The Japanese economy stalled in the third quarter, official data showed on Monday, as it was hit by Iran war-fuelled inflation, bad weather and an earthquake. The zero quarter-on-quarter growth in July-September was short of forecasts for 0.1 per cent expansion and was down from the 0.4 per cent recorded in the previous three months. Persistently high inflation triggered by the Middle East conflict was a factor in sluggish consumer spending, while a weak yen pushed up the cost of imported goods. On an annualised basis, the economy shrank 0.1 per cent, against expectations of 0.2 per cent growth. Higher oil prices have swollen Japan’s import bill and led to higher prices for consumers. That partly helped explain why real private consumption fell 0.3 per cent in the third quarter, extending a similar drop in April-June. But the weather was likely a factor too, “as typhoons and heavy rain kept consumers away from shops,” according to Taro Kimura of Bloomberg Economics. Net exports were also down — acting as another drag on growth — in part because of an earthquake that struck the southwestern island of Kyushu in July, leading to factory closures. However, chief researcher at Mitsubishi UFJ Research and Consulting, Shumpei Fujita, said prior to the data release that “considering the headwinds from the worsening situation in Iran, the domestic economy is maintaining its resilience.” The latest growth figure is unlikely to dissuade the Bank of Japan from raising interest rates again in December as inflationary pressure builds, analysts say. “In fact, it looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we’ve been anticipating as inflation is about to surge,” Thieliant said. The central bank last month said inflation had hit its two per cent target, more than 13 years after it adopted the goal in a bid to pull the economy out of deflation. Japan is expected to fall to sixth place among the world’s largest economies in 2027, with India and Germany overtaking it, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund.
